steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat with the palm facing up.
Rest your dominant closed hand, thumb up, on top of that flat palm.
Keep the position steady, or lift it slightly.
tip: “Helps” is signed with the base HELP sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat with the palm facing up.
Rest your dominant closed hand, thumb up, on top of that flat palm.
Keep the position steady, or lift it slightly.
tip: “Helping” is signed with the base HELP sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat with the palm facing up.
Rest your dominant closed hand, thumb up, on top of that flat palm.
Keep the position steady, or lift it slightly.
tip: Past form of “Help” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Raise your dominant hand, palm facing outward, fingers together.
Push it firmly forward toward the person or thing you want to stop.
Keep your expression serious to match a 'halt' command.
tip: “Stopping” is signed with the base STOP sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Raise your dominant hand, palm facing outward, fingers together.
Push it firmly forward toward the person or thing you want to stop.
Keep your expression serious to match a 'halt' command.
tip: Past form of “Stop” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Bend the index finger of your dominant hand into a hook.
Start with the hand in front of your body.
Pull the bent finger toward yourself, like beckoning.
tip: “Comes” is signed with the base COME sign.

steps: Bend the index finger of your dominant hand into a hook.
Start with the hand in front of your body.
Pull the bent finger toward yourself, like beckoning.
tip: “Coming” is signed with the base COME sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat, palm facing your chest.
Slide it down your chest, then twist your wrist so the palm turns outward.
tip: “Wants” is signed with the base WANT sign.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat, palm facing your chest.
Slide it down your chest, then twist your wrist so the palm turns outward.
tip: “Wanting” is signed with the base WANT sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat, palm facing your chest.
Slide it down your chest, then twist your wrist so the palm turns outward.
tip: Past form of “Want” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: BSL uses the same sign for NEED as for WANT.
Hold your dominant hand flat, palm facing your chest.
Slide it down your chest, finishing with a small outward twist of the wrist.
tip: “Needs” is signed with the base NEED sign.

steps: BSL uses the same sign for NEED as for WANT.
Hold your dominant hand flat, palm facing your chest.
Slide it down your chest, finishing with a small outward twist of the wrist.
tip: “Needing” is signed with the base NEED sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: BSL uses the same sign for NEED as for WANT.
Hold your dominant hand flat, palm facing your chest.
Slide it down your chest, finishing with a small outward twist of the wrist.
tip: Past form of “Need” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat with fingers together, thumb folded across (a closed flat hand).
Tap your chest with it once or twice.
tip: “Likes” is signed with the base LIKE sign.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat with fingers together, thumb folded across (a closed flat hand).
Tap your chest with it once or twice.
tip: “Liking” is signed with the base LIKE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat with fingers together, thumb folded across (a closed flat hand).
Tap your chest with it once or twice.
tip: Past form of “Like” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Make a fist with your thumb sticking out.
Tap the side of your head with your thumb, repeating the tap.
tip: “Knows” is signed with the base KNOW sign.

steps: Form the BSL letter M with your dominant hand.
Tap it against your open non-dominant palm twice.
tip: Plural of “Mother” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold out your non-dominant hand with just the index and middle fingers extended.
Tap those two fingers twice with the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand — this is the BSL letter F signed twice.
tip: Plural of “Father” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your body, one resting over the other, arms bent as if cradling something.
Rock your hands gently from side to side, like holding a baby.
tip: Plural of “Baby” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Clasp your non-dominant hand with your dominant hand in front of your body.
Make a small up-and-down bobbing movement with the clasped hands.
tip: Plural of “Friend” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend only the index finger of your dominant hand.
Brush it along your chin, moving from your dominant side toward the other side.
tip: Plural of “Boy” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Make a closed fist with your index finger pointing up.
Brush the finger down your cheek twice.
tip: Plural of “Girl” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Bring your fingertips and thumb together into a bunched shape.
Tap the bunched fingers against your mouth twice.
tip: “Eats” is signed with the base EAT sign.

steps: Bring your fingertips and thumb together into a bunched shape.
Tap the bunched fingers against your mouth twice.
tip: “Eating” is signed with the base EAT sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a loose C shape, as if holding a cup.
Lift the hand up to your mouth.
Tip your wrist toward your face, as though taking a drink from the cup.
tip: “Drinking” is signed with the base DRINK sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold both hands open in front of your body, palms facing toward you.
Move the hands alternately up and down.
Add a grimace that matches the severity of the pain.
tip: Plural of “Pain” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Flatten both hands, palms facing inward.
Cross both hands over your chest on the left side.
Give a small warm press inward with a gentle smile.
tip: “Loves” is signed with the base LOVE sign.

steps: Flatten both hands, palms facing inward.
Cross both hands over your chest on the left side.
Give a small warm press inward with a gentle smile.
tip: “Loving” is signed with the base LOVE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Flatten both hands, palms facing inward.
Cross both hands over your chest on the left side.
Give a small warm press inward with a gentle smile.
tip: Past form of “Love” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Bend the fingers of your dominant hand so the fingertips point downward.
Tap your fingertips against the far side of your chest.
Then tap them against the near side of your chest.
tip: Plural of “Morning” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands open in front of your body with palms facing inward.
Move both hands downward together until they finish flat and horizontal.
tip: Plural of “Night” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant arm out in front of you.
With your dominant thumb, draw a small cross on top of your opposite forearm.
tip: Plural of “Hospital” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out flat, palm facing up.
Tap the inside edge of that palm twice with your dominant index finger.
tip: Plural of “Bathroom” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands up in front of you with fingers closed, as if gripping a steering wheel.
Move both hands up and down in opposite directions, like turning the wheel.
tip: Plural of “Car” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both flat hands up at an angle in front of you, fingertips pointing up.
Bring the fingertips together so your hands form the shape of a roof.
tip: Plural of “House” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your dominant hand up with index and middle fingers extended together.
Bend your wrist side to side while moving your hand downward.
tip: Plural of “School” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a fist, knuckles facing forward.
Raise the closed fist to the side of your chin, knuckles pointing outward.
Tap the knuckles against your chin twice, with two crisp beats.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your cheek throughout both taps.
Nod once as you finish, so it reads as a definite number.
tip: Plural of “Number” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like a page.
Form a V with the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand.
Sweep the V fingertips down across the palm, zigzagging from wrist toward fingers.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while the fingertips glide over the page.
Fix your gaze on the moving fingertips, as if your eyes are reading along.
tip: “Reads” is signed with the base READ sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like a page.
Form a V with the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand.
Sweep the V fingertips down across the palm, zigzagging from wrist toward fingers.
Keep your dominant palm facing down while the fingertips glide over the page.
Fix your gaze on the moving fingertips, as if your eyes are reading along.
tip: “Reading” is signed with the base READ sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Open your dominant hand beside your head, fingers together and thumb relaxed.
Hold the open hand just to the side of your temple, palm angled inward.
Draw the hand slightly backward while your fingers close together into a pinch.
Keep the motion small and close to the head, finishing with pinched fingertips.
Keep a thoughtful, attentive expression, as if an idea has just landed.
tip: “Learns” is signed with the base LEARN sign.

steps: Open your dominant hand beside your head, fingers together and thumb relaxed.
Hold the open hand just to the side of your temple, palm angled inward.
Draw the hand slightly backward while your fingers close together into a pinch.
Keep the motion small and close to the head, finishing with pinched fingertips.
Keep a thoughtful, attentive expression, as if an idea has just landed.
tip: “Learning” is signed with the base LEARN sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Open your dominant hand beside your head, fingers together and thumb relaxed.
Hold the open hand just to the side of your temple, palm angled inward.
Draw the hand slightly backward while your fingers close together into a pinch.
Keep the motion small and close to the head, finishing with pinched fingertips.
Keep a thoughtful, attentive expression, as if an idea has just landed.
tip: Past form of “Learn” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Curve both hands into full C shapes, thumbs opposing the fingertips.
Hold the two C hands in front of your chest, a few inches apart.
Tip the hands toward each other in alternating inward pouring motions.
Keep the pouring smooth and rhythmic, like decanting between two beakers.
Wear a curious, inquisitive expression — science is about wondering.
tip: Plural of “Science” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Press both flat hands together in front of your chest, palms touching.
Open and close the hands repeatedly, like flicking through a book's pages.
Travel both hands sideways as they open and close, covering a short distance.
Keep your palms facing each other through every opening motion.
Glance along the path of the moving hands, as if scanning a shelf.
tip: Plural of “Library” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, index finger and thumb slightly apart.
Hold the C hand upright in front of your torso, fingers pointing forward.
Move the hand straight down once, in one clean stroke.
Keep the C handshape steady and the palm facing sideways through the drop.
Mouth the word 'student' silently, since the same sign also means person and pupil.
tip: Plural of “Student” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into relaxed fists in front of your body.
Bring the fists together so the outer edges meet at chest height.
Tap the hands against each other twice, with two light, even beats.
Keep both palms facing inward and the wrists relaxed through the taps.
Keep the taps small and crisp — big swings start to look like clapping.
tip: Plural of “Paper” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Pinch your dominant thumb and index finger into a small circle.
Spread your remaining fingers open behind the pinched thumb-and-index circle.
Hold the hand in front of your chest and draw a question mark in the air.
Trace the hook first, then dot it with a short downward flick.
Raise your eyebrows and lean slightly forward, the classic questioning face.
tip: Plural of “Question” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like paper.
Pinch your dominant index fingertip against your thumb, as if holding a pen.
Make small side-to-side scribbling motions across the open palm surface.
Keep your dominant palm angled sideways and the strokes quick and light.
Keep the writing hand moving — a still pen on a palm reads as pointing.
tip: “Writes” is signed with the base WRITE sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like paper.
Pinch your dominant index fingertip against your thumb, as if holding a pen.
Make small side-to-side scribbling motions across the open palm surface.
Keep your dominant palm angled sideways and the strokes quick and light.
Keep the writing hand moving — a still pen on a palm reads as pointing.
tip: “Writing” is signed with the base WRITE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Extend the index fingers of both hands, tucking the other fingers away.
Raise both hands to the sides of your head, fingers pointing upward.
Hold the hands briefly at temple height, framing your head.
Keep both palms facing each other across the sides of your head.
Mouth the word 'teacher' silently, since regional variants of this sign exist.
tip: Plural of “Teacher” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Pinch both thumbs against index fingers to form two F handshapes.
Hold both F hands in front of your body, a few inches apart.
Move the hands together in a small horizontal clockwise circle.
Keep the F circles intact and the motion smooth through the loop.
Soften your face with a warm expression — family is an affectionate sign.
tip: Plural of “Family” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curve your dominant hand into a C, index finger and thumb slightly apart.
Hold the C hand upright before your torso, fingertips pointing forward.
Bring the hand straight down once, in a single smooth stroke.
Hold the C shape firm and the palm facing sideways during the drop.
Mouth the word 'person' silently, since the same sign also means student and pupil.
tip: Plural of “Person” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close your dominant hand, leaving the index finger extended straight upward.
Hold the extended fingertip against the side of your chin, close to the jawline.
Brush the finger along your chin, moving from your dominant side across to the other side.
Keep the finger pointing upward and the palm angled toward your face through the brush.
Mouth the word 'son' clearly, since the sign shares its handshape with 'boy'.
tip: Plural of “Son” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend the index and middle fingers of your dominant hand, closing the rest into a fist.
Hold the hand at chest height in front of your body, fingers pointing upward.
Glide the hand sideways to one side, then back again, in a small smooth motion.
Repeat the sideways glide two or three times, as if indicating two people.
Keep your palm facing forward and your expression neutral and inclusive.
tip: Plural of “Parent” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Pinch the fingertips and thumb of your dominant hand together into a bunched shape.
Bring the bunched hand up toward your mouth, fingertips pointing inward.
Touch the fingertips lightly to your lips, as if placing food into your mouth.
Repeat the touch once more with the same small, crisp motion.
Keep your palm facing sideways and look toward your hand as you sign.
tip: Plural of “Food” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curve the fingers and thumb of your dominant hand into a C, like holding a small cup.
Lift the C hand to chin height in front of your mouth.
Tilt your wrist back and forth repeatedly, as if sipping from a cup.
Keep the motion gentle and rhythmic, with two or three easy tilts.
Mouth 'coffee' to fix the drink, since cup shares this handshape.
tip: Plural of “Coffee” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curve the fingers and thumb of your dominant hand into a C shape.
Raise the C hand to mouth height, as if holding a cup in your hand.
Tilt the hand back slightly toward your lips, as if taking a sip.
Repeat the small tilt once or twice with an easy, even rhythm.
Mouth the word 'cup' clearly, since coffee shares this sipping motion.
tip: Plural of “Cup” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Extend the index and middle fingers of both hands, keeping each pair together.
Point both finger-pairs downward in front of your body at chest height.
Bounce both hands up and down together in small, quick movements.
Keep the bounce lively, repeating two or three playful beats.
Smile as you sign — dog is a cheerful, bouncy sign.
tip: Plural of “Dog” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl the fingers of both hands into claw shapes, thumbs held out.
Hold both clawed hands in front of your chest, palms angled downward.
Circle the hands forward in repeated round motions.
Keep the circles smooth and even, two or three full loops.
Keep your gaze forward — the looping claws suggest all kinds of creatures.
tip: Plural of “Animal” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into fists and stack one on top of the other.
Hold the stacked hands in front of your body at waist height.
Move the hands up and down together, as if holding a pair of reins.
Keep the movement small and steady, like gentle tugs on the reins.
Lean slightly forward with an alert expression, as if riding.
tip: Plural of “Horse” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Open your dominant hand fully, fingers together and thumb relaxed.
Hold the open hand out in front of you at waist height.
Push the hand forward while twisting your wrist from side to side.
Keep the twists small and repeated, like a fish wriggling forward.
Point your fingertips forward so the hand glides like a swimming fish.
tip: Plural of “Fish” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Curl the fingers of both hands into claw shapes, thumbs tucked in.
Touch the fingertips of both clawed hands to your cheeks.
Drag both hands outward from your cheeks in one smooth pull.
End with the hands slightly apart at face width, palms angled outward.
Narrow your eyes slightly, as if picturing the whiskers you traced.
tip: Plural of “Cat” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close your non-dominant hand into a fist and hold it steady.
Lay your flat dominant hand on top of the fist, palm facing down.
Stroke the dominant hand forward over the fist, as if petting an animal.
Repeat the stroke a second time with the same gentle motion.
Keep your face soft and warm — you are stroking a small animal.
tip: Plural of “Pet” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands open and flat in front of your torso, fingers together.
Touch the middle fingertips of both hands lightly against your chest.
Drag both hands slowly upward across your chest without lifting them away.
Keep your palms facing inward toward your body for the whole movement.
Mirror the feeling with your face — soft and open for good feelings, tense for bad ones.
tip: “Feels” is signed with the base FEEL sign.

steps: Hold both hands open and flat in front of your torso, fingers together.
Touch the middle fingertips of both hands lightly against your chest.
Drag both hands slowly upward across your chest without lifting them away.
Keep your palms facing inward toward your body for the whole movement.
Mirror the feeling with your face — soft and open for good feelings, tense for bad ones.
tip: “Feeling” is signed with the base FEEL sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Form a 'V' with your dominant index and middle fingers, folding the rest away.
Raise the hand up beside your eye, keeping the fingertips pointing upward.
Push the V handshape straight forward, away from your face.
Turn your palm to face yourself, keeping the fingers vertical through the push.
Look along your hand as it moves, so your gaze follows the 'seeing' direction.
tip: “Sees” is signed with the base SEE sign.

steps: Form a 'V' with your dominant index and middle fingers, folding the rest away.
Raise the hand up beside your eye, keeping the fingertips pointing upward.
Push the V handshape straight forward, away from your face.
Turn your palm to face yourself, keeping the fingers vertical through the push.

steps: Hold both hands as flat blades, fingers together and straight, thumbs tucked.
Rest the flat edge of your dominant hand across the top of the other hand.
Tap the bottom edge of the upper hand against the top edge of the lower hand.
Keep both palms facing sideways, fingertips pointing across your body.
Repeat the small tapping motion twice, keeping your expression businesslike.
tip: “Working” is signed with the base WORK sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold both hands as flat blades, fingers together and straight, thumbs tucked.
Rest the flat edge of your dominant hand across the top of the other hand.
Tap the bottom edge of the upper hand against the top edge of the lower hand.
Keep both palms facing sideways, fingertips pointing across your body.
Repeat the small tapping motion twice, keeping your expression businesslike.
tip: Past form of “Work” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, folding the others away.
Raise the fingertip to the side of your forehead, near the temple.
Tap the side of your head once or twice with the fingertip.
Keep your palm facing inward and the finger pointing at the head.
Hold a thoughtful expression — the sign needs the 'thinking' face to land.
tip: “Thinks” is signed with the base THINK sign.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, folding the others away.
Raise the fingertip to the side of your forehead, near the temple.
Tap the side of your head once or twice with the fingertip.
Keep your palm facing inward and the finger pointing at the head.
Hold a thoughtful expression — the sign needs the 'thinking' face to land.
tip: “Thinking” is signed with the base THINK sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat, palm up, fingertips pointing forward.
Close your dominant hand into a fist, leaving the thumb extended.
Swipe the extended thumb sharply downward across the open palm.
Keep the open hand steady as the base while the thumb does the work.
Use a decisive expression — the firm swipe marks the beginning of something.
tip: “Starts” is signed with the base START sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat, palm up, fingertips pointing forward.
Close your dominant hand into a fist, leaving the thumb extended.
Swipe the extended thumb sharply downward across the open palm.
Keep the open hand steady as the base while the thumb does the work.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat, palm up, fingertips pointing forward.
Close your dominant hand into a fist, leaving the thumb extended.
Swipe the extended thumb sharply downward across the open palm.

steps: Close both hands into tight fists, keeping the thumbs tucked inside.
Hold both fists in front of your chest at shoulder width.
Pump the fists up and down in quick alternation, like pumping arms while running.
Keep the fists vertical, moving about a hand's length with each pump.
Lean your body slightly forward — the lean sells the running motion.
tip: “Running” is signed with the base RUN sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Pinch the tip of your dominant thumb and index finger together, leaving the other fingers extended.
Bring the pinched fingertips to the corner of your mouth, just beside your lips.
Push the hand forward away from your mouth in one smooth stroke, keeping the pinch closed.
Hold your palm angled roughly toward the person you are asking.
Mouth the word 'ask' as you push forward, with your eyebrows slightly raised.
tip: “Asks” is signed with the base ASK sign.

steps: Pinch the tip of your dominant thumb and index finger together, leaving the other fingers extended.
Bring the pinched fingertips to the corner of your mouth, just beside your lips.
Push the hand forward away from your mouth in one smooth stroke, keeping the pinch closed.
Hold your palm angled roughly toward the person you are asking.
Mouth the word 'ask' as you push forward, with your eyebrows slightly raised.
tip: “Asking” is signed with the base ASK sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Pinch the tip of your dominant thumb and index finger together, leaving the other fingers extended.
Bring the pinched fingertips to the corner of your mouth, just beside your lips.
Push the hand forward away from your mouth in one smooth stroke, keeping the pinch closed.
Hold your palm angled roughly toward the person you are asking.
Mouth the word 'ask' as you push forward, with your eyebrows slightly raised.
tip: Past form of “Ask” — signed with the base sign; time is shown separately, not on the verb.

steps: Make an open pinched handshape with your dominant hand, thumb and fingertips held apart.
Start the hand a short distance in front of your chest, palm roughly facing sideways.
Pull the hand back toward your chest in one decisive motion while closing the pinch shut.
Keep the movement single and firm, like plucking one option out of the air.
Pair it with a decided expression and mouth 'choose' as your hand closes.
tip: “Chooses” is signed with the base CHOOSE sign.

steps: Make an open pinched handshape with your dominant hand, thumb and fingertips held apart.
Start the hand a short distance in front of your chest, palm roughly facing sideways.
Pull the hand back toward your chest in one decisive motion while closing the pinch shut.
Keep the movement single and firm, like plucking one option out of the air.
Pair it with a decided expression and mouth 'choose' as your hand closes.
tip: “Choosing” is signed with the base CHOOSE sign — ASL/BSL marks ongoing action on the sign, not with a separate word.

steps: Hold both hands open and flat in front of your chest, palms facing toward you.
Cross your hands at the wrists while keeping the palms facing inward.
Sweep both hands upward and outward in a wide arc, as if tracing the rising sun.
Finish with your hands apart at about shoulder height, palms still facing you.
Keep a neutral expression and mouth 'day' as the arc completes.
tip: Plural of “Day” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat in front of your chest, palm facing upward.
Point your dominant index finger down into the hollow where the base hand's thumb meets the palm.
Hold the position steady for a beat — YEAR is fingerspelled as the letter Y, not signed.
Mouth the word 'year' clearly while you hold the letter shape.
tip: Plural of “Year” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Raise both hands into the fingerspelling space in front of your chest.
Fingerspell J, then A, then N with the two-handed BSL alphabet, keeping the flow smooth.
Let your dominant hand work over the steady non-dominant base hand for each letter.
Mouth the word 'January' as you fingerspell so your reader catches the month.
tip: Plural of “January” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close both hands into fists with only the index fingers extended straight.
Hold your non-dominant fist out in front of you with the forearm pointing outward.
Start your dominant fist at the elbow end of your non-dominant forearm.
Slide the dominant fist along the forearm until the two fists meet.
Keep both palms facing sideways and mouth 'week' as the fists touch.
tip: Plural of “Week” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady as your base hand.
Fingerspell O, then C, then T using the two-handed BSL alphabet.
Keep the three letters flowing in one continuous, unbroken motion.
Mouth 'October' as you land on the final T.
tip: Plural of “October” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand steady as the base hand at chest height.
Fingerspell F, then E, then B with the two-handed BSL alphabet.
Keep the letters tight and flowing in one continuous movement.
Mouth 'February' as you finish the B.
tip: Plural of “February” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady in front of you at chest height.
Form the fingerspelled letter F with your dominant hand above the base hand.
Move the dominant fingers in a small circular motion over the stationary base hand.
Keep the circles tight and repeated, palm facing down toward the base hand.
Mouth 'Friday' clearly while you circle the F.
tip: Plural of “Friday” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and steady as your base hand.
Form the fingerspelled letter M with your dominant hand above it.
Tap the M down onto the base palm twice in quick succession.
Keep the base hand still, palm facing up, while the M bounces off it.
Mouth 'Monday' clearly on the double tap.
tip: Plural of “Monday” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands open and flat in front of your body, palms turned toward each other.
Keep the open hands about a handspan apart at chest height.
Bring the palms together until they meet in a soft, controlled double contact.
Tap palm-to-palm twice without pausing long between the two touches.
Keep your elbows relaxed at your sides through both contacts.
Mouth the word 'Sunday' clearly as the palms meet for the second contact.
tip: Plural of “Sunday” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a closed hand and hold it steady in front of you.
Make a clenched fist with your dominant hand and extend only the index finger.
Hold the dominant index finger in the air above your non-dominant hand.
Rotate the fingertip in a steady clockwise circle, like a clock hand sweeping.
Keep the circle small and the non-dominant hand completely still.
Mouth 'hour' with a neutral expression as the finger circles.
tip: Plural of “Hour” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and steady as your base hand in front of your chest.
Form the fingerspelled letter T with your dominant hand above the base hand.
Tap the T down onto the base palm twice in quick succession.
Keep the base hand still, palm facing up, while the T bounces off it.
Mouth the word 'Tuesday' clearly as the letter T lands its double tap.
tip: Plural of “Tuesday” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands flat and open in front of your body at chest height.
Keep your non-dominant hand stationary with the palm facing forward.
Move your dominant hand in smooth circular loops in front of the steady hand.
Let the circles stay wide and even, like marking out a rounded day off.
Keep the base hand flat and still while the other hand does the circling.
Mouth the word 'Saturday' clearly while your dominant hand keeps circling.
tip: Plural of “Saturday” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and steady as your base hand in front of your chest.
Fingerspell the two-handed letter T with your dominant hand over the base hand.
Flow straight into the two-handed letter H without any pause or break.
Let the dominant hand reshape from T to H in one continuous, fluid motion.
Keep the base hand steady and mouth 'Thursday' through the whole movement.
tip: Plural of “Thursday” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and steady as your base hand in front of your chest.
Form the fingerspelled letter W with your dominant hand above the base hand.
Tap the W down onto the base palm twice in quick succession.
Keep the base hand still, palm facing up, while the W bounces off it.
Mouth the word 'Wednesday' clearly as the letter W lands its double tap.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a closed flat hand, fingers pressed together.
Raise the hand to your forehead, starting on the non-dominant side of your face.
Brush the flat hand across your forehead in one smooth horizontal sweep.
Keep the palm brushing lightly against the skin as it crosses to the other side.
Finish the sweep near your dominant temple with the hand still flat.
Mouth the word 'summer' with a warm, relaxed expression as the sweep finishes.
tip: Plural of “Summer” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Clench both hands into fists and hold them parallel in front of your body.
Raise the fists to chest height with your arms held stiffly.
Shake both fists back and forth in quick, short movements.
Keep the fists close together and parallel while they shiver side to side.
Let your arms stay tense to suggest cold, shuddering arms.
Mouth the word 'winter' as you shake, keeping your shoulders slightly hunched.
tip: Plural of “Winter” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a fist with only the index finger extended straight.
Rest the extended index finger on top of your non-dominant wrist.
Hold the non-dominant hand flat and steady in front of you.
Move the index fingertip in small, short clockwise circles above the wrist.
Keep the circles tiny and regular, like a clock ticking through seconds.
Mouth 'minute' with a neutral expression as the finger ticks.
tip: Plural of “Minute” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands open in front of your body at chest height, palms facing inward.
Curve both hands around an imaginary ball floating between them.
Trace the full round shape of the globe with both open hands.
Keep the palms curved and relaxed as they outline the ball together.
Finish with both hands cupping the finished ball shape in front of you.
Mouth the word 'world' with a neutral, open expression as you hold the ball shape.
tip: Plural of “World” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.

steps: Hold both hands in open flat handshapes in front of your body.
Turn both palms to face toward you at chest height.
Sweep both hands around in big, smooth circular motions through the air.
Let the circles grow wide and gusty, as if a strong wind is blowing.
Move both hands together in the same direction through the swirl.
Mouth 'wind' with slightly puffed cheeks as the gusts turn.
tip: Plural of “Wind” — sign the base sign (often repeated) for more than one.
